P1.evidence: The only call in the batch with a setter, and the read-back was done properly and at length — training history, the Valencia marathon, the plateau, the injuries, the IT job and the diet were all played back with "Just so I know, I pay attention" and "Kyla also mentioned...". The prospect confirmed each point, which is exactly the effect the check is for. Against that, no frame was set at all: no four-part structure, no expectations for the call, and no "does that work?". The open question did get asked, just late and well into discovery — "what would be your main reason to look into kettlebells? Because everybody has different reasons".

P2.evidence: The strongest baseline in the batch. Age, height and weight all asked directly. Work asked and quantified including its sedentary nature and exact hours. Injuries interrogated hard and over several minutes — the mechanism of the back injury, whether he had seen a doctor, whether he feels it daily, when the pattern of small injuries began ("Can you put like a number on that?" / "Three, four years ago") and whether there had been surgeries. Training week fully mapped including content, split and session length. Results from current training asked in the right form — "How do you feel after a session? Like energized, drained?" — which is what surfaced the plateau. Nutrition asked and followed up on protein sources. Energy asked properly with a morning and afternoon breakdown. Two gaps: health conditions, own or hereditary, were never asked at all, and sleep was covered only by a leading question about quality ("you would say your sleep is good, like you feel recovered?") with no quantity.

P3.evidence: The one-thing question was asked almost verbatim — "if we could change one thing about where you're physically at right now, what would it be for you?" — and answered with mobility. The bridge to the deeper why was pushed twice rather than accepted first time: "why is that important to you?" then, against "because it's something I want", the rep came back with "I know that you want it, but why?", which produced the real answer about priorities and self-respect. The future-state question was asked and then extended into the best moment of the call — "what else would you like to be doing that you're not doing right now because of the lack of energy?" — which surfaced that he wants to leave IT and farm. Where it fell short: "who else does that impact?" was never asked, the drive-through to family and legacy stopped at a passing question about children, and the reflect-back was a flat summary ("So more energy, more intensity, and mobility") rather than the "this isn't really about X, it's about Y" reframe. The prospect had to add "and less small injuries" himself.

P4.evidence: Well run. What he had tried came out in full — a decade of dumbbell splits, a year of Olympic rings with a personal trainer, the self-taught morning mobility routine. What happened with each was asked, including why he stopped with the trainer ("Because he went to Dubai") and why he never replaced him. Why it did not stick was pushed on directly: "you didn't try to do any program on your own, like with progressing weights? ... Why not?" producing "I felt content with my routine. I felt it was enough" and then "But now it's not enough." The prospect named the mechanical gap himself — "just building muscles, but not doing any mobile work" — which is exactly what the check asks for. The single blocker was never quite landed; the rep pressed the injury pattern hard ("why do they happen?") and left it unresolved. P4f is marked not applicable because the scripted reframe assumes the prospect cannot stick to things alone, and this one demonstrably can — ten years unbroken, self-directed. Asking it would have been the wrong question.

P5.evidence: The only call in the batch where the two-year question was actually asked: "if you don't actually make this change with how you work out, how do you feel it would be in the future, in the next two, three years?" The prospect answered "No, I have to make a change" — and the rep immediately abandoned the frame and switched to the positive future ("if you got exactly what you wanted..."). None of the follow-through ran: no settle-for, no why-not, no line in the sand. The consequence was raised and then dropped at the exact moment it would have started doing work, which is a recurring shape for this rep.

P6.evidence: The cleanest commitment check in the batch and run in the right order, before any number. The belief question was asked in full — "If you had the right training, the nutrition dialed in, and accountability and guidance from Trevor, do you agree you would get to your goals of getting stronger, being more intense, and eventually more happy?" — then the all-in question followed: "if we can figure out the details, are you going to be fully committed to actually showing up and doing the work, which is going to be hard?" answered "100 percent". Crucially he then pushed once more with "No doubt about it?", which surfaced a genuine reservation the prospect had been sitting on ("is three times a week, 30 to 40 minutes, enough?"). That is the check working as designed.

P11.evidence: No close was attempted on either product. The call ended with the rep agreeing to email details of the cheaper option for a decision over the weekend.

objection_plays.detail: The most complete run of this play in the batch. Isolation ran twice, properly — "is it the money thing or you're not just money" then "You sure? There's nothing else? Only the financial side of things?" Normalisation ran — "Most of the clients that we work with just put it on a credit card... but for some, if there is like a financial obstacle, we can work our ways around that." Consent was asked for explicitly — "Would you be open to talk about it?" Then the financial picture was built in the scripted order: cash on hand ($3,000), what is left monthly after bills ($200), credit cards (none), investments and crypto (none). Available credit and used-versus-available were not asked because there are no cards to ask about. The only missing move is the "you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place" reframe. Notably the rep did the honest thing with the answer: he concluded no plan could bridge a $6,000 gap on $3,000 of savings and $200 a month, and did not discount the core offer to force it.

"I would need to think about it" landed at 00:50:42. The rep ran the shared isolation step and nothing else from the play — no "do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to your goal", no "thinking isn't the problem, deciding is", no identity move. Scored partial rather than miss because the isolation immediately established the deferral was purely financial ("No, it's just the money. Nothing about anything else you said before"), which makes routing to OC the correct decision rather than an omission.

Two separate fear triggers. The first — "three times a week, 30 to 40 minutes, is it enough?" — was answered with warmth and a personal guarantee rather than any scripted move, and it resolved. The second, and the more important one, came after the downsell: "do you think it's still easy enough to learn by myself without someone correcting me?" The rep answered with a condition about not ignoring pain, plus the community. Neither the certainty question, the bridge, the plane nor the burned-before move was used.

"I would like to start when I feel good with my back... I want to start when I'm completely good with my body" is a not-the-right-time trigger in form. The rep did not run the play, and that was the right call — every scripted move ("things never slow down", "the longer you wait the harder this gets", "the only thing you can control is right now") would have been pressure applied against an unassessed acute spinal injury. Recorded as a miss for accuracy, but the coaching note is the reverse of usual: the script needs an explicit medical carve-out so reps are not choosing between the playbook and the prospect's safety.
The girlfriend features throughout but never as a decision gate; he treated the purchase as entirely his own.

The clinical gap, and here it is acute rather than historical. The prospect disclosed a ten-day-old back injury he has never had assessed, which he already worsened by returning to training too early, and which the rep himself suspected might be a disc. There is no screen, no clearance requirement and no stop condition anywhere in the process. The rep asked a genuinely good question — "what needs to happen with your body that you will finally understand, oh, maybe I should check out what's going on with a doctor?" — and then never converted it into a condition of purchase or of starting.

There is no scripted downsell. When the financial picture ruled out the core offer, the rep improvised a route to Primal University at $200 a month or $2,000 a year — a real product at a price the playbook does not contain. He was honest about what it is not ("this is not one-on-one with Trevor") and about the caveat that it is not tailored, which is to his credit. But there is no guidance on when a downsell is appropriate, and in this case it moved a man with an active back injury from a supervised product with video form correction to an unsupervised one without it.

notes: Process-wise this is the rep's best call in the batch by a distance — setter notes read back, a near-complete baseline, real persistence on the deeper why, the only two-year consequence question anyone asked, a proper commitment check before the number, and a full open-wallet conversation that ended in an honest no-discount conclusion. Two corrections. First, having asked the two-year question he abandoned it in one beat; sit in the answer and run settle-for and why-not before moving to the upside. Second, and this outranks everything else on the call: he identified an unassessed acute back injury, raised the possibility of a disc himself, and then presented, priced and downsold without ever making medical clearance a condition of starting. That should be a hard stop in the process, not a matter of rep judgement.
